title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess  and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
description:
Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

From her elegant French gowns to a colossal painting of her jewels, from the Egyptian artifacts she acquired for her fledgling museum to a Hawaiian skirt she may or may not have purchased immediately before her suspicious death, Jane! presents various idiosyncratic artifacts of Stanford lore—many shown for the very first time, and very likely for the last.

IMAGE: Napoleon T. Sarony, Portrait of Jane Lathrop Stanford, 1871. Photograph with charcoal touch up, 55 ½ x 45 in. Cantor Arts Center, Stanford University, Stanford Family Collections, JLS.18217

title: A Vision of Paris: The Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford
description:
Stanford University Libraries presents A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford, on view in the Peterson Gallery and Munger Rotunda of the Cecil H. Green Library from September 22, 2026 to January 24, 2027. 

Roxane Debuisson (1927–2018) dedicated sixty years to documenting the transformation of the city of Paris during the nineteenth century.  If Roxane Debuisson could not stop the changes she saw underway in the late 20th century, she could at least preserve the city’s earlier history through images, literature, guidebooks, and other documents. 

Her lifelong project helped to document Paris during the nineteenth century, especially the city’s rapid changes from the 1850s to the 1870s, when Emperor Napoleon III and his prefect of the Seine, Baron Eugène Haussmann, transformed the city with new boulevards, green spaces, and public utilities, and fostered innovations in commercial and cultural practices. 

A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford draws upon the extensive array of commercial almanacs, prints, postcards, commercial ephemera, stereographs, manuscripts, historic photographs, and other items that are a part of the Roxane Debuisson Collection of Paris history, circa 1789-1970, acquired by the Department of Special Collections at Stanford University Libraries in 2020. These materials place Paris as the birthplace of political, commercial, and urban innovations, and as a city defined by the tension between its historical past and its continuous reinvention. The exhibit highlights the city’s rapid changes and their diverse causes, while suggesting the collection’s vast possibilities for both research and instruction.

This exhibition is curated by Sarah Sussman, Assistant University Librarian for Collections and Services & Curator of French and Italian Collections, Stanford University Libraries, and Chloe Summers Edmondson, Assistant Professor of French at the University of Miami. Produced and designed by Deardra Fuzzell, with assistance from Kylee Jo Diedrich, Sofia McGullam Ornelas, and Pasha Tope.

A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford will be open to the public. Registration at the entrance with a valid government ID is required to enter the Cecil H. Green Library and view the exhibit.

title: Gallery Conversations | JANE!
description:
Join us for casual in-gallery conversations in our special exhibition, JANE!, facilitated by our Museum Engagement Guides. Enjoy a spotlight tour focusining on a single object, followed by an open conversation. 

Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

From her elegant French gowns to a colossal painting of her jewels, from the Egyptian artifacts she acquired for her fledgling museum to a container of her beauty cream excavated from her Palo Alto mansion destroyed in the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, JANE! presents various idiosyncratic artifacts of Stanford lore—many of them shown for the very first time—and very probably for the last.

We gratefully acknowledge lead support for JANE! provided by Pamela and David Hornik. Sustained support generously provided by The C. Diane Christensen Fund for African Art.

---

Public tours are free for all. Please check in at the visitor services desk* in the main museum lobby.

*If you plan to bring a large group with you (10 people or more), please notify us one week in advance via this form so we can inform our Guides. Thank you!

title: Earth Systems Program Coterm Info Session
description:
Interested in advancing your studies in Earth Systems? Join us on for a hybrid information session to explore Earth Systems’ Coterminal Master’s Degrees, learn about the application process, hear from current students, and get your questions answered!

MS in Earth Systems

Explore complex environmental challenges at the intersection of human activities and natural Earth system changes. Tailor your studies to your interests while developing the knowledge and skills to address critical social and environmental issues and sustainability challenges.

 

 MA in Environmental Communication

Learn to communicate complex environmental challenges through advanced theoretical frameworks, analytical tools, and practical skills. Build your expertise through specialized coursework, independent project work, and a professional practicum.

For more information, visit the Earth Systems Coterminal Programs page.

title: Patty Chang: surfacing
description:
Event Details:

In surfacing, Patty Chang engages the ocean as a physical, geopolitical, and symbolic space, inviting you to consider the work of collection and recollection. Chang’s multimedia sculptural practice brings together archaeological remains from Point Alones Chinese Fishing Village (now the site of Stanford’s Hopkins Marine Station), fish specimens from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology, and archival materials documenting the lives of Chinese fisher families on the Monterey Peninsula.  In a critical encounter with the scientific enterprise of survey and collection, Chang surfaces the mysterious intimacies, forgotten collaborators, and unrecorded histories that haunt the Pacific and its coast.

Patty Chang: surfacing culminates a year-long residency through the Denning Visiting Artist program, during which Chang was embedded at Stanford’s Hopkins Marine Station. The exhibition’s central sculptural work is a porcelain massage table that was originally commissioned for the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s exhibition Monstrous Beauty: A Feminist Revision of Chinoiserie and now travels to Stanford to take new form as a surface upon which to dry squid. This act of transmutation connects histories of the ocean, labor, and racial and gendered violence: the transpacific migration of porcelain and people; the scientific collection of marine specimens; the labor of fishing and drying squid; and the 2021 Atlanta Spa Shootings.  It is a project of grief, memorial, rage, and disobediance—an invitation to think with the deep, and to watch for what begins to rise.

On view: September 17, 2026 - February 8, 2027
Anderson Collection, 314 Lomita Dr
Gallery Hours: Thursday-Monday, 11am–5pm
Curated by Kelsey Chen and Marci Kwon 

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

Patty Chang: surfacing is the first solo artist commission by Stanford’s Asian American Art Initiative.  It is organized by the Anderson Collection at Stanford University and co-curated by Kelsey Chen, interdisciplinary theorist, artist, PhD Candidate in Modern Thought & Literature, and Marci Kwon, Associate Professor of Art & Art History and Marta Sutton Weeks Faculty Scholar in the Humanities.  The exhibition is made possible with support from the Robert H. N. Ho Family Foundation Global, a Humanities Seed Grant from Stanford Public Humanities, the Stanford Arts Roberta Bowman Denning Visiting Artist Fund, and generous support for programs and operations from William Reller & Kristin E. Klint, Anderson Student Engagement Fund, and museum members. We extend special thanks to the staff of Hopkins Marine Station, Quock Mui Foundation, and the Point Alones Chinese Fishing Village descendant community.

 

VISITOR INFORMATION

The Anderson Collection at Stanford University is located at 314 Lomita Drive, Stanford, CA 94305, on the Stanford campus, adjacent to the Cantor Arts Center. Patty Chang: surfacing is on view in the Wisch Family Gallery. The museum is open Monday and Thursday–Sunday, 11 a.m.–5 p.m., and closed Tuesday and Wednesday. Visitor parking is available in designated areas, with contactless payment managed through ParkMobile.

Alternatively, take Caltrain to the Palo Alto Transit Center and connect to the free Stanford Marguerite Shuttle. The exhibition is open to Stanford affiliates and the general public. Admission is free, and advance reservations are not required.

Connect with the Anderson Collection! Subscribe to our mailing list and follow us on Instagram and Facebook.
